name: Granada
info: Granada is a city of Andalusia in southern Spain, at the foot of the Sierra Nevada, an Iberian and Roman settlement that became a major city of al-Andalus in the 11th century and the capital of the last Muslim-ruled state in the Iberian Peninsula.

facts.founded: An oppidum called Ilturir was founded by the Iberian Bastetani tribe around 650 BCE; Arab sources such as al-Idrisi regard the Zirid ruler Zawi ben Ziri as the founder of the city of Granada in the 11th century.
facts.where: At the foot of the Sierra Nevada in Andalusia, Spain, at the confluence of the Darro, Genil, Monachil and Beiro rivers, on the Vega de Granada plain, 50 km from the Mediterranean coast.
facts.known: The Zirid taifa and its Jewish vizier Samuel ha-Nagid; the Nasrid Emirate, the last Muslim-ruled state in the Iberian Peninsula; the Alhambra; the surrender of 2 January 1492; the Albaicín quarter; the University of Granada, founded in 1531
facts.today: Granada is the capital of the province of Granada in the autonomous community of Andalusia, Spain, with a population of about 233,000.

t: Granada grew from an Iberian oppidum and the Roman town of Iliberis, and in the 11th century the Zirids made the former Jewish town of Ġarnāṭa the main city of the region in place of Ilbīra.
From 1228 the Nasrid dynasty ruled the Emirate of Granada from the city, built the Alhambra on the Sabika hill, and held out as the last Muslim-ruled state in the peninsula until 2 January 1492.
After the conquest the Muslim population was forced to convert or leave, the mosques became churches, and the city took on a Catholic and Castilian character under Charles V and his successors.
dyk: In 1812 French troops leaving Granada tried to dynamite the whole Alhambra and blew up eight towers before the Spanish soldier José Garcia disabled the remaining fuses.
ev: The Iberian Bastetani found the oppidum of Ilturir
Zawi ben Ziri founds the Zirid Taifa of Granada, and Ġarnāṭa replaces Ilbīra as the main city
Muhammad I Ibn al-Ahmar begins the Alhambra
Muhammad XI surrenders Granada to the Catholic Monarchs
Charles V founds the University of Granada
The Second Morisco Rebellion begins in the Alpujarras and leads to the expulsion of most moriscos from the Kingdom of Granada

sections.origins:
Granada stands at the foot of the Sierra Nevada, at the confluence of four rivers, the Darro, the Genil, the Monachil and the Beiro, on the Vega de Granada. The fertile soil of the plain is irrigated by streams that rise in the Sierra Nevada, and the city lies at an average elevation of 738 m, 50 km from the Mediterranean coast. The region has been populated since at least 5500 BCE, and finds in the city show that the site, including the area around the present Gran Vía de Colón, was inhabited in the Bronze Age.

The most ancient ruins belong to an oppidum called Ilturir, founded by the Iberian Bastetani tribe around 650 BCE. The name Elibyrge is also attested for the area, and the settlement later became known as Iliberri or Iliberis. In 44 BCE Iliberis became a Roman colony, and in 27 BCE a Roman municipium named Florentia Iliberritana, 'Flourishing Iliberri'. Scholars have long debated whether present-day Granada is the same settlement as Roman Iliberis, but excavations on the Albaicín hill have uncovered a significant Roman town there. Little is known of the city between the end of the Roman era and the 11th century. A Christian synod, the Synod of Elvira, met near the area around 300 CE, and its exact location is not established.

The Arabic name Ġarnāṭa is of uncertain meaning and origin. It probably first appeared in the 9th century and is found in Arabic sources from the 10th. Proposed meanings include 'hill of strangers' and 'hill of pilgrims'; another theory derives it from Latin granum, 'seed', or a scarlet colour.
sections.growth:
After the Zirids moved their residence to Ġarnāṭa in the 11th century, the city grew in a short time into one of the most important cities of al-Andalus. It spread from the Albaicín to include the Sabika hill, the Mauror hill and part of the surrounding plains, and was fortified with walls enclosing about 75 hectares. Under the Zirid kings Habbus ibn Maksan and Badis, Granada was the centre of Jewish Sephardi culture and scholarship. Granada also served as an administrative capital of Almoravid rule in al-Andalus, and the artistic and archaeological remains suggest that the city thrived under the Almoravids and declined under the Almohads.

Under the Nasrids the city expanded again. Muslim refugees from the territories conquered by Castile and Aragon swelled the population, and new neighbourhoods grew around the Albaicín, named after refugees from Baeza, and in Antequeruela, named after refugees from Antequera after 1410. Because of the heavy tribute paid to Castile, Granada's economy specialised in high-value goods. Its ports traded with the Genoese and Catalans and, to a lesser extent, the Venetians, Florentines and Portuguese, and the kingdom exported silk and dried fruits and received gold from sub-Saharan Africa and the Maghreb.

The city was an intellectual centre as well, especially under Muhammad V, whose court was served by Ibn Khaldun and Ibn al-Khatib. Ibn Battuta visited in 1350 and called Granada the 'metropolis of Andalusia and the bride of its cities'. When it surrendered in 1492 its population was 50,000.
sections.rulers:
The Umayyad conquest of Hispania, beginning in 711, brought the region under Moorish control and established al-Andalus. The most important settlement in the area was then Madīnat Ilbīra, near present-day Atarfe, while a smaller settlement and fortress named Ġarnāṭa stood on or near the Albaicín and had a mainly Jewish population. At the beginning of the 11th century the Zirids, a Sanhaja Berber group, held the province of Elvira in the service of the Caliphate of Córdoba. When the caliphate collapsed after 1009 and the Fitna began, their leader Zawi ben Ziri established the independent Taifa of Granada. The Almoravids ruled Granada from 1090 and the Almohads from 1166.

In 1228 Idris al-Ma'mun, the last effective Almohad ruler in al-Andalus, left the peninsula. Ibn al-Ahmar (Muhammad I) established the Nasrid dynasty, which ruled the Emirate of Granada and was the last and longest reigning Muslim dynasty in the peninsula. In 1246 he became a vassal of Ferdinand III of Castile, and Granada was thereafter a tributary state of Castile, although wars between the two often interrupted this. The Nasrids sometimes sought the help of the North African Marinids, whose interventions in the peninsula ended after the Battle of Río Salado in 1340.

On 2 January 1492 Emir Muhammad XI, known to the Spanish as Boabdil, surrendered the emirate to the Catholic Monarchs, Ferdinand II of Aragon and Isabella I of Castile, after the last episode of the Granada War. In 1810 Napoleon's army occupied Granada during the Peninsular War, and the occupation lasted until 1812.
sections.life:
Until the 11th century Granada had a mixed population of Christians, Muslims and Jews. Under Habbus ibn Maksan, the Jewish administrator Samuel ha-Nagid became his secretary in 1020 and later took charge of the army under Badis. Daniel Eisenberg writes that Granada was then the centre of Sephardic civilisation at its peak and that all of the greatest figures of 11th-century Hispano-Jewish culture are associated with it, among them Moses Ibn Ezra, Judah ha-Levi and Ibn Gabirol.

Under the Nasrids the population became more uniformly Muslim and Arabic-speaking than before. The heart of the city was its Great Mosque, on the site of the present cathedral, and the commercial district known as the qaysariyya, the Alcaicería. Beside it stood the only major madrasa built in al-Andalus, the Madrasa al-Yusufiyya, founded in 1349. The Maristan, a hospital, was built in 1365 to 1367 and demolished in 1843. The Alhambra functioned as a self-contained palace-city with its own mosque, hammams, fortress and quarters for workers and servants.

In the 16th century immigrants from other regions of Castile came for the economic opportunities of the newly conquered city. By 1561 the population included more than 30,000 Christian immigrants and about 15,000 moriscos, and most of the moriscos lived in the Albaicín. Most mosques were converted into churches during and after the mass conversions of 1500. The town council was established on 23 September 1500, and in 1531 Charles V founded the University of Granada on the site of the madrasa built by Yusuf I.
sections.crises:
According to Arabic sources the old town of Ilbīra was razed during the Fitna and was not restored. After the death of Samuel ha-Nagid, his son Joseph proved to lack his father's diplomacy and brought on the 1066 Granada massacre, which ended the golden age of Jewish culture in Spain.

The terms of the surrender of 1492, set out in the Treaty of Granada, allowed the Muslim inhabitants to keep their faith and customs. The Alhambra Decree of 31 March 1492 nevertheless forced all Jews in Spain to convert or be expelled within four months. By 1499 Cardinal Francisco Jiménez de Cisneros had begun a programme of forced baptisms, a direct violation of the treaty. It provoked the Rebellion of the Alpujarras of 1499 to 1501, after which the Crown of Castile rescinded the treaty and ordered Granada's Muslims to convert or emigrate. Most converted and became moriscos.

In December 1568 the Second Morisco Rebellion broke out in the Alpujarras. Although the city's moriscos played little part in it, Philip II ordered the expulsion of most of them from the Kingdom of Granada, and the Albaicín was depopulated. The final expulsion of all moriscos from Castile and Aragon was carried out between 1609 and 1614. In the 17th century the population stagnated at about 55,000.

French troops occupied the Alhambra as a fortified position and damaged it, and in 1812 they attempted to blow up the whole complex. When the Spanish Civil War broke out in 1936 Granada joined the Nationalist uprising, and local resistance from the working classes of the Albaicín was violently repressed.
sections.legacy:
The Alhambra was begun in 1238 by Muhammad I Ibn al-Ahmar on the site of earlier fortresses and of the 11th-century palace of the vizier Samuel ibn Naghrillah. The Comares Palace and the Palace of the Lions date mostly from the reigns of Yusuf I and Muhammad V in the 14th century. After 1492 it became the royal court of Ferdinand and Isabella, and in 1526 Charles V commissioned a Renaissance palace beside the Nasrid ones. In the 18th century it fell into severe neglect. Washington Irving lived in Granada in 1830, and his Tales of the Alhambra, published in 1832, brought it international attention. UNESCO inscribed the Alhambra and the Generalife in 1984 and extended the site to the Albaicín in 1994.

The Christian city left its own monuments. The cathedral was begun in the early 16th century over the Great Mosque, and Diego Siloé gave it a Renaissance design. The Catholic Monarchs chose Granada as their burial place by a decree of 13 September 1504, and the Royal Chapel, begun in 1505, holds their tombs. The Charterhouse was founded in 1506 and built over the following 300 years. The Sacromonte hill has been the old neighbourhood of the Romani, who settled in Granada after the conquest, and its abbey was founded in the 17th century.

Granada is today the capital of the province of Granada in Andalusia, with about 233,000 inhabitants. The Albaicín keeps much of its medieval street plan, parts of the Zirid and Nasrid walls, the Bañuelo bathhouse and cisterns of the Islamic water system, and the pomegranate, granada in Spanish, is the city's heraldic device.

summary: Granada, in Andalusia at the foot of the Sierra Nevada, grew from an Iberian and Roman settlement into a major city of al-Andalus under the Zirids. From 1228 it was the capital of the Nasrid emirate, the last Muslim-ruled state in the peninsula, until the surrender of 1492.
